Very interesting, I've taken a quick skim and here are my thoughts:

This paper assumes central authority ("the bank") to prevent double spending (it refers to this as "multiple spending").

To protect against multiple spending, the Bank maintains a database of spent electronic coins. Coins already in the database are to be rejected for deposit. If the payments are on-line, this will prevent multiple spending. If off-line, the best we can do is to detect when multiple spending has occurred. To protect the payee, it is then necessary to identify the payer. Thus it is necessary to disable the anonymity mechanism in the case of multiple spending.

There was a lot of public discussion around such schemes in the 90's

Most notably, and IMO the clearest ancestor to bitcoin is the proposed system called b-money: https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/B-money

http://www.weidai.com/bmoney.txt

But like this paper no solid solution was arrived at for preventing double spending without trust in a central authority.

The key innovation of Bitcoin was the innovation of the blockchain as a means of preventing double spending without trusting a central authority.

If you have any interest in this sort of thing at all, I highly recommend reading the original Bitcoin white paper.

https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf
